common_name: Thunberg's Daylily (Late-Blooming Fragrant Yellow Species Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Thunberg's daylily blooms notably later than most species and hybrid daylilies, extending the bloom season into midsummer, and its flowers open in late afternoon and stay open into evening.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Native to Japan and Korea, Hemerocallis thunbergii is a tall wild species bearing lightly fragrant, lemon-yellow flowers held well above the foliage on slender scapes, blooming later in the season than most daylilies and, unusually, opening in late afternoon and remaining open into the evening rather than closing by dusk like typical daytime-blooming daylilies. Its late bloom time makes it a useful parent for extending daylily flowering into midsummer and a valuable collector's plant in its own right. The clump forms a tidy, upright mass of grassy foliage and is slow to spread, rarely needing division more than once every several years to remain vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Many-Flowered Daylily (Late Small-Flowered Branching Species Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Many-Flowered Daylily blooms very late in the season and produces an unusually large number of small flowers per scape.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Native to China, Hemerocallis multiflora is a late-blooming wild species that lives up to its name by producing an unusually high number of small, golden-orange flowers on each heavily branched flower scape, sometimes twenty or more buds per stem, extending well into late summer and early fall after most other daylilies have finished blooming for the year. This late bloom time and heavily branched flowering habit have made it valuable breeding stock for extending the daylily season and increasing flower count in modern hybrids. The clump forms a dense mass of narrow, grassy foliage and multiplies steadily, benefiting from division every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and flowering.

common_name: Singing in the Rain Itoh Peony (Apricot-Orange Blushed Pink Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Singing in the Rain bears semi-double flowers that open a warm apricot-orange and soften as they age, often blushed with pink toward the petal edges, a soft, changeable color progression that gives the plant an extended season of visual interest as older and newer blooms open at different stages. Like other Itoh hybrids it combines the flower form and color range of tree peonies with the reliable die-back-to-the-ground habit and cold hardiness of herbaceous peonies, holding its heavy blooms upright on strong stems without staking. Its deeply cut, glossy foliage stays attractive well past bloom, giving good structure in the border through summer, and the plant is best left undisturbed for years once established, since Itoh peonies resent division and transplanting.

common_name: Sequestered Sunshine Itoh Peony (Pale Yellow Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Sequestered Sunshine produces large, semi-double flowers in a soft, pale butter-yellow, a gentler tone than the bright lemon-yellow of Bartzella, giving it a quieter presence in the border that pairs easily with pastel companions. Its strong, woody-based stems hold the large flowers upright without staking, and the deeply cut, disease-resistant foliage stays attractive well after bloom finishes, providing good structure through summer and into fall. Like other Itoh hybrids it tolerates more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight herbaceous peonies, performing into zone 9 with afternoon shade, and dies back to the ground each winter like an herbaceous peony rather than persisting as a woody shrub.

common_name: Old Faithful Itoh Peony (Deep Red Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Old Faithful bears large, semi-double to double flowers in a deep, rich red, one of the darkest colors available among Itoh hybrids, held on strong, woody-based stems that support the heavy blooms without staking or flopping. Its glossy, deeply cut foliage stays clean and disease-resistant through summer well after bloom finishes, giving good structure to the border for the rest of the growing season. Like other intersectional hybrids it combines tree peony flower form and color range with the cold-hardy, die-back-to-the-ground habit of herbaceous peonies, tolerating more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight Paeonia lactiflora cultivars. Divide only when absolutely necessary, since Itoh peonies resent disturbance and can take a couple of seasons to rebloom fully after moving.
